title: Why were the Ligots acquitted?

stances.claim: The Ligots were acquitted not because they were innocent of having unexplained wealth -- the Senate hearings made that plain -- but because the prosecution failed to convert those perceived facts into legal facts admissible under the strict rules of evidence: the bank deposits were excluded by the Bank Secrecy Law, the AMLC memo was misdirected, key property documents were not formally offered, and the California properties were unauthenticated by PH consular officials.
stances.rhetorical_move: perceived-vs-legal-facts distinction explaining the gap between public knowledge and judicial outcome

stances.claim: The Bank Secrecy Law's absolute confidentiality (RA 1405) admits only four exceptions -- written consent, impeachment, court order in bribery/dereliction cases, and where the money itself is the litigation subject matter -- and none of these applied to the BIR's tax evasion charge, making the deposit evidence categorically inadmissible regardless of how persuasive the Senate hearings were.
stances.rhetorical_move: exception-enumeration showing categorical inadmissibility, not discretionary exclusion

stances.claim: The nation can still mitigate its defeat through three other venues: the Sandiganbayan asset forfeiture case, the Makati RTC AMLA case, and the BIR's independent right to collect taxes despite the criminal acquittal -- provided the prosecution learns its lesson on converting perceived facts into legal facts.
stances.rhetorical_move: remaining-venues optimism with conditional caveat (prosecution must improve)

stances.claim: The rules of evidence -- though complicated -- exist precisely to filter out bias, popular belief, and error in the search for truth, and the Ligot acquittal is a cost of that filtering system, not a failure of it; the appropriate response is better prosecutorial preparation, not procedural shortcuts that would compromise the rules.

notable_anecdotes: Quotation of the Inquirer's Jan 22 editorial title 'The lucky Ligots' and its accusation that someone produced 'so remiss and shoddy a work that gave the Ligots exactly the lucky break they needed to squeak out of the law's grasp' -- using the paper's own indignant editorial framing to set up the legal analysis that follows.

The detailed property catalog -- Malaybalay Bukidnon land, Essensa East Forbes Condo Taguig, two Paseo Parkview Tower II condos (registered to one Miguela L. Paragas), 5-hectare Tanay Rizal property held in trust for military officers, Anaheim and Buena Park California properties -- each falling for a different technical evidentiary reason, demonstrating that the prosecution failed across the entire asset base in different ways.

The cross-reference to CJ's own Jan 20 column 'Commenting on high-profile cases' -- making the Ligots acquittal a concrete demonstration of the perceived-vs-legal-facts framework articulated two weeks earlier.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban answers the Inquirer's Jan 22 editorial demanding accountability for the Court of Tax Appeals' acquittal of Gen. Jacinto Ligot and his wife Erlinda -- whose 2001-2004 income tax returns and SALNs were dwarfed by hundreds of millions of pesos in bank deposits and properties exposed in 2011 Senate hearings. Examining the CTA's 83-page decision by Justice Ma. Belen M. Ringpis-Liban, he explains that the prosecution failed to convert the Senate-hearing 'perceived facts' into legal facts: the bank deposit evidence was categorically excluded by the Bank Secrecy Law (RA 1405), whose absolute confidentiality admits only four exceptions (written consent, impeachment, court order in bribery/dereliction cases, money-as-litigation-subject), none applicable to the BIR's tax evasion charge; the AMLC memo was wrongly directed to the Makati RTC rather than the CTA; the Malaybalay Bukidnon land and Essensa East Forbes Condo titles were never formally offered in evidence; the two Paseo Parkview Tower II condos showed no nexus to the registered owner Miguela L. Paragas; the 5-hectare Tanay property was held in trust for military officers; and the Anaheim and Buena Park, California properties were not authenticated by PH consular officials as required. He closes that 'all is not lost' -- the asset forfeiture case in the Sandiganbayan, the AMLA case in the Makati RTC, and the BIR's independent tax collection right all remain available, provided the prosecution learns its lesson on converting perceived facts into legal facts; the rules of evidence, 'though complicated, were designed to discover the truth, free from bias, popular belief and error.'
